subject: larry-ellison
research_tasks: Read Softwar (Matthew Symonds, 2003, with Ellison's own footnotes) and The Difference Between God and Larry Ellison (Mike Wilson, 1997) in a licensed copy. Both exist in print; the online archive copies were lending-restricted. The repair opened three reviews of Wilson's book (Kirkus S43, Publishers Weekly S44, Computergram S45) and the article now states what they report, but the book's own wording and sourcing are unverified. In Wilson, check: who says he lived in the 'South Side ghetto' and to which reporters; what he said about degrees; the childhood friend's exact words; the sentence 'he had to humiliate them' and what episodes support it; the Citizen Kane theme. In both books look for first wife Adda Quinn's and the co-founders' testimony and for Ellison's footnoted replies about his father, Ray Lane's departure and his need to win. The typing claims C47, C58, C136 and C138 stay unresolved until this is done; if the books show the Lane ouster was about credit or that the 'humiliate' line has no episodes behind it, reopen the lead with --refresh --expanded-review.

PRE-RELEASE: Check the USC speech line 'That way I could completely control my work environment' (C50) against USC's official video and cite a timestamp. Until then the body and the FAQ attribute it to a published transcript.

PRE-RELEASE: Open the Washington Post report of May 2022 and the Fair Fight v. True the Vote filing on the November 14, 2020 call, and establish whether Ellison or Oracle was asked for comment or has ever commented (C80). The edit removed the draft's unsupported sentence that Oracle did not respond to the Post.
PRE-RELEASE: Check the Delaware Chancery docket for Robbins v. Ellison (filed July 2026) for its status after the October 6, 2026 closing (C32, C84, C124).

PRE-RELEASE: Open Bloomberg Businessweek's June 13, 2022 cover story on Lanai and the New York Times Magazine feature of September 2014 for firsthand resident testimony on both sides and any response from Ellison or his island company. The edit cut the secondhand resident quotation and now reports only The Nation's argument, labelled as argument (C121).
PRE-RELEASE: Open the Forbes interview of April 1, 2020 and confirm Ellison's remarks on the Trump fundraiser, which the article quotes through TheWrap (C118, C119).

Corroborate the September 1993 SEC settlement ($100,000 fine, no admission) and the $24 million shareholder settlement against the SEC's release or a major newspaper report; the only opened source is one trade-press item (C110). Check whether Ellison was personally named.

Establish the outcome of the federal securities class action over the January 2001 trades, which Computerworld reported as still pending in 2005. Until then the insider-trading FAQ says only what the Delaware opinion and the California settlement reports establish (C127).

Still to do, because the edit and repair stages may only write their three outputs (verify-06): add these to docs/writing-system/people-controversies.json and flip to required, then run pnpm controversies:check: Oracle revenue overstatement, shareholder suits and SEC settlement (1990-1993); Adelyn Lee suit and conviction (1993-1997); detectives and Microsoft trash (2000); insider-trading suits, Delaware ruling and California settlement (2001-2005); PeopleSoft hostile takeover (2003-2004); surveillance remarks (2002-2024); Lanai (2012 onward); Trump fundraiser, employee protest and November 2020 call (2020-2022); Robbins v. Ellison (2026). All nine are on the page. Add two more as open: Oracle's 2016 purchase of NetSuite, and the 2013 America's Cup cheating penalty.

Write the 2013 America's Cup penalty into the storm section in one plain paragraph. Opened in the repair (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_America's_Cup, section 'Cheating penalty', 2026-11-12): an international jury found Oracle Team USA guilty of cheating in the 2012 America's Cup World Series warm-up by placing lead pellets in its 45-foot catamarans; three team members were expelled, the team was fined $250,000 and its first two race wins in the 2013 Match did not score. It was left off the page only because the body is at the word ceiling; the body and FAQ still mention the 2013 win without it, which a refresh should correct. Find a primary report and any statement from Ellison or the team. The death of Artemis sailor Andrew Simpson in May 2013 was not opened.
Verify job cuts after the PeopleSoft purchase in an opened source before stating a figure; the article gives only CBS's attributed forecast.

The email in which Ellison wrote that he 'decided not to veto' Lee's firing is quoted by Kalat from Softwar. It was left out of the article until the book is read; add it beside his denial once confirmed.
Confirm the 1998 race results against the Cruising Yacht Club of Australia's official table; Wikipedia is the only opened source that separates first-to-finish from the handicap winner (C65).

Confirm the split of the Knowledge Universe founding investment (Wikipedia says $250 million from Ellison; Education Week and The Nation give $500 million combined) before stating Ellison's share (C98).

Find independent corroboration of the 1995 plan to buy Apple (Walter Isaacson's Steve Jobs). The Castle Rock story, in which Ellison says he deferred to Jobs, was left out of the article as his own 2016 reconstruction of a talk with a friend who had died.
Confirm marriages, dates and children against a major news source; Wikipedia is the only source so far. The article states only that he had been married three times by 2002.

Look for first-person testimony from people close to him who are not rivals or ousted executives: Safra Catz, Ed Oates, David or Megan Ellison, long-time sailing crew. Current third-party evidence skews hostile.
Take the exact Musk-Ellison text messages from the Twitter v. Musk court exhibit; outlets quote them differently (C25).
Confirm the original broadcast date of the 60 Minutes II segment; the article cites only the CBS web publication of February 2004 (C13).

Before saying more about philanthropy, open reporting on the Ellison Institute of Technology and Ellison's July 2025 statement. The article quotes only the 2010 Giving Pledge letter as stated intent (C122).
Resolve whether David Ellison is CEO or co-CEO (with Ynon Kreiz) of Skydance; S21 and S22 differ. The article states neither.

Length: the repaired body is 4,487 words by the contract counter (limit 4,500, target 3,500). The repair added about 330 words of evidence the verifier required and cut about 310. Cut in the repair, each recoverable from the named source: the 1997 Gulf War answer about competitors (S02, was C90); the 1997 'self-discovery, the discovery of my own limits' line (S02, was C09); the block quotation of the garbage offer, now one inline sentence (S08); 'We found out, but the question was, how could we prove it?' (S03); 'making deals with God, if he would return her to me' (S02); Fortune's 'to his son's rescue' headline (S20, was C123); the rename of the merged company to Skydance (S21, was C82); the body paragraph on the September 2025 co-CEOs, now in the FAQ only (S25); the standalone Type 6 paragraph, whose curfew test moved to the surveillance section. Not added for length: the Citizen Kane theme of Wilson's book and its link to Jobs's 'Rosebud' (S45). A refresh that reads the books should restructure the last third and bring the body under 4,000.

NetSuite (verify-06): Oracle offered $9.3 billion for NetSuite on July 28, 2016 while Ellison owned nearly 40 percent of it, and both boards set up independent committees (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NetSuite, opened 2026-11-12). The shareholder derivative suit and its outcome could not be opened in the repair: the Reuters report was behind a CAPTCHA and the Delaware opinions on Justia returned 403 or 404. It is not on the page because a paragraph without the court outcome would be unfair to him. Open the Delaware Court of Chancery post-trial opinion (2023) and any Delaware Supreme Court ruling, then add one paragraph to 'What the control costs other people' with the outcome label and his side's response.

Computergram's review of Wilson (S45) also summarises two allegations that are not on the page because each is third-hand with no response: that Ellison had no-longer-favoured employees fired just before their stock vested, and that he presented a prenuptial contract to his third wife hours before the wedding. Check both in Wilson's book and against any response before using either.

sources.title: Smithsonian Oral and Video Histories: Excerpts from an Oral History Interview with Lawrence Ellison
sources.speaker: Larry Ellison (interviewed by Daniel Morrow, Computerworld Smithsonian Awards Program)
sources.locator: Sections 'A South Side Boy', 'Looking East', 'Building Oracle' (Genghis Khan story), 'A Good Place to Work', 'The Creative Act', 'On Heroes'
sources.excerpt: "When I started Oracle, what I wanted to do was to create an environment where I would enjoy working. That was my primary goal." ... "I thought, well, I don't need leadership to do that. I can run a company out of business all by myself. So I thought, next time, if the company was going to go down, I was going to be out front." ... "If I had only realized that I was an engineer and a builder by nature." ... "So I was a lousy student, but a good builder."
sources.context: Edited oral-history transcript (about 12,400 words) recorded when Ellison was 51 and Oracle had about $2 billion in sales. The live americanhistory.si.edu page returned a service-unavailable error on 2026-11-11, so the archived copy was opened and read in full. The transcript is labelled 'Excerpts' and was edited by Thomas J. Campanella, so wording is an edited record of speech. The Genghis Khan passage is Ellison retelling a Japanese executive's words and complaining that the New York Times printed the line as his own. Typos in the original ('tired to', 'aduthood') should not be reproduced as his speech.

sources.title: Larry J. Ellison interview: Prophet of Software (Academy of Achievement)
sources.speaker: Larry Ellison (Academy of Achievement interviewer unnamed)
sources.locator: Interview tab, dated 'Baltimore, Maryland May 22, 1997'. Questions: 'Looking back on your childhood...', 'How did this affect you?', 'You seem to thrive on a certain kind of balance...', 'Have you ever been deeply afraid?', 'What about fear of failure?', 'People have accused you of launching some brutal attacks...'
sources.excerpt: "I think most overachievers are driven, not so much by the pursuit of success, but by the fear of failure. Unless failure gets very close and very nearby that fear doesn't reach profound levels, but it drives us. It drives me to work very hard. It drives me to make sure that my life is orderly, that I'm in control of my company, or in control of the airplane or boat or what-have-you, so that I'm not at risk of failure." ... "When fashion and the pursuit of love is in conflict with reason, too often fashion and the pursuit of love usually win. In my case, it didn't."
sources.context: Long edited interview (about 6,000 words) given at the 1997 Academy of Achievement program, when Ellison was 52. Page opened and read in full; the interview text sits in the page HTML under the Interview tab. The widely shared pull-quote 'Great achievers are driven...' is the Academy's display version; the transcript says 'most overachievers'. The interview mentions 'a very nasty boat race, from Sidney to Hobart' with a 14-hour storm; given the May 1997 date this cannot be the fatal December 1998 race and probably refers to his 1995 win. The page was last revised September 11, 2025.

sources.title: Playboy Interview: Larry Ellison
sources.speaker: Larry Ellison (interviewed by David Sheff for Playboy); introduction by Playboy editors and Sheff
sources.locator: Sheff's own site, headed 'This article was originally published in September 2002'. Introduction (Hardball, Siebel and Conway quotes, Adelyn Lee summary); Q&A exchanges on the garbage investigation, Bill Gates and Netscape, firings in 1991, the Sydney-Hobart race, the Lee accusation, his adoptive father, his sister's question, birth family, non-conformity, the Internet bet, marriage
sources.excerpt: "In theory, parents grant their children unconditional love. Other love has to be earned. If you don't get unconditional love early on, you have a great void in your life. Depending on how you adapt, you can get very good at trying to earn the love of others." ... "Without love from your parents, the love of others becomes a large part of your life. You either learn how to get it or you try to get it through your achievements." ... "I didn't know they were going to go through Bill's garbage, but that doesn't bother me at all." ... "I shouldn't seek to control her anymore than I would want her to control me."
sources.context: Full-length magazine interview (about 9,000 words) conducted at Oracle headquarters when Ellison was 58, republished on the interviewer's site. Opened and read in full. Some Playboy questions are missing from the republished text, so a few answers appear without their prompt. The line 'Privacy is an illusion' and the Siebel and Conway quotes come from the editors' introduction, not from Ellison's answers in this interview, and are secondhand. The interview says he had been married three times and was engaged to Melanie Craft.

sources.title: The World's Most Competitive Man (60 Minutes II)
sources.speaker: Larry Ellison and Ray Lane (interviewed by Charlie Rose, CBS News)
sources.locator: CBS News web write-up of the broadcast segment, full article. Passages: 'addicted to winning', the sister's question, 'never amount to anything', 'all the disadvantages required for success', Ray Lane on Oracle culture, 'personal vanity', Golden Gate Bridge exchange
sources.excerpt: "When I was a kid, my sister walked into my room and said, 'Larry, which is more important to you – to be admired or be loved?' And I said, 'Well, for me personally? To be admired.' She looks at me, smiles, 'Wrong,' and walks out. It took me a little while to realize that all of us want to be loved." ... "It was an alternative greeting as opposed to, 'Hi, how are you?' or, 'How did it go at school today,'" ... "I admit to it, mea culpa. An awful lot of it is personal vanity."
sources.context: Network web article summarizing a broadcast interview when Ellison was 59, during Oracle's hostile bid for PeopleSoft. Opened and read in full. The page date is February 23, 2004; the exact air date was not confirmed. The article paraphrases as well as quotes: in the sentence about his father, only the words 'never amount to anything' are inside quotation marks. Ray Lane speaks as an executive Ellison pushed out in 2000 and is not a neutral witness. CBS calls the Genghis Khan line his 'favorite saying'; Ellison's answer in the same article attributes it to a Japanese executive.

sources.title: Full Transcript: Larry Ellison's Speech at USC Commencement 2016
sources.speaker: Larry Ellison (commencement address, University of Southern California); transcript by The Singju Post
sources.locator: Full speech transcript. Passages: pre-med and dropping out at 21; first wife and the sailboat; 'A huge burden of fear had been lifted'; 'completely control my work environment'; the 1995 Castle Rock walk with Steve Jobs; 'give nearly all of it away'
sources.excerpt: "I put together a plan to start my own company. That way I could completely control my work environment." ... "For the first time, I was certain that I was going to survive in this world. A huge burden of fear had been lifted." ... "I attempted to create an environment that I could completely control. Instead I was running a company with thousands and thousands of people that was growing so fast that it was impossible for anyone to control."
sources.context: Prepared speech delivered at age 71 to USC graduates, in a week when he announced a $200 million gift to USC. The transcript is a third-party transcription (page dated September 25, 2024); USC's own transcript page returned a 404. Key lines are confirmed by USC's same-day news report (S06). A commencement address is a polished self-narrative written for an audience, not spontaneous testimony. The Jobs dialogue is Ellison's reconstruction 21 years after the walk; Jobs had died in 2011.

sources.title: Oracle's Larry Ellison urges graduates to pursue their own dreams as USC marks 133rd commencement
sources.speaker: USC News (reporting and quoting Larry Ellison)
sources.locator: News report, first ten paragraphs quoting the speech
sources.excerpt: "Once again, I was unable to live up to expectations of others," ... "But this time, I was not disappointed in myself for failing to be the person they thought I should be. Their dreams and my dreams were different. I would never confuse the two of them again."
sources.context: The university's own same-day report of the address. Opened. It independently confirms the wording of several lines in the third-party transcript (S05), including 'Whatever the underlying reasons, I was unable to make myself into the person that I thought I should be'. It is not independent of the speech itself.

sources.title: The next richest man in the world
sources.speaker: Andy Serwer, Fortune (quoting Larry Ellison, Steve Jobs, Andy Grove and unnamed Oracle executives)
sources.locator: Archive republication of the Nov. 13, 2000 cover story. Opening scene in Ray Lane's former office; the dumpster passage; the 'Rosebud' paragraph; the biography and 'pirate ship' paragraphs; the Andy Grove quote
sources.excerpt: "When Apple founder and CEO Steve Jobs (whom Ellison repeatedly refers to as his best friend) is asked what he thinks is the driving motivation of his pal, he chuckles, thinks for a moment, and then whispers into the phone: "Rosebud."" ... "He works very hard at his bad-boy image," says Ellison's pal, former Intel C E O Andy Grove.
sources.context: Contemporaneous magazine profile reported when Ellison was 56 and briefly close to passing Bill Gates in wealth. Opened; the archive copy ends partway through the original article and contains OCR spacing errors ('C E O'). Jobs's one-word answer is a joke that points at a lost childhood and is not an explanation. Descriptions such as 'His own CFO calls him a dictator' and 'going through wives and top executives like pairs of boots' are Serwer's wording. The 'unsavory, yucky' line about the detectives is Ellison's. The profile also cites Wilson's biography: 'According to The Difference Between God and Larry Ellison, by Mike Wilson, Ellison was considered smart but bridled under authority and was not a particularly great student.' It says he 'grew up working class in an apartment building in Chicago'.

sources.title: Ellison offers Gates all his rubbish
sources.speaker: Thomas C. Greene, The Register (quoting Larry Ellison at a press conference)
sources.locator: News report of Ellison's June 28, 2000 press conference, first four paragraphs
sources.excerpt: "All we did was to try to take information that was hidden and bring it into the light," Ellison said. "That's a public service." ... "We will ship our garbage to Redmond, and they can go through it. We believe in full disclosure."
sources.context: Next-day report of the press conference Ellison held after it emerged that Oracle's hired firm, Investigative Group International, had tried to buy the office trash of the Microsoft-funded Association for Competitive Technology. Opened. The Register writes in a sardonic house style and notes that Oracle funded its own advocacy groups. The original New York Times and Wall Street Journal reports were not opened.

sources.title: CNN Sunday Morning: Recounting Sydney/Hobart Yacht Race Hurricane
sources.speaker: Larry Ellison and G. Bruce Knecht (interviewed by Miles O'Brien, CNN)
sources.locator: Rush transcript, full segment. Ellison's answers on why he entered, the satellite picture, fear, and 'Hillary and Everest'
sources.excerpt: "I was a much better sailor in 1998 than I was in 1995 and I wanted to see how much better I really was in another Sydney/Hobart." ... "Unfortunately, the weather got worse faster than I got better." ... "It's not because it's there. It's because we're there and we're curious if we can do it." ... "Fear doesn't really accomplish very much."
sources.context: Live television interview two and a half years after the December 1998 race in which six sailors died. Opened and read in full. CNN marks it a rush transcript that may contain errors; the host says 'Hillary and Everest' and Ellison repeats it, though the famous line is George Mallory's. Knecht, author of The Proving Ground, appears beside him and is an independent reporter of the race.

sources.title: CNN Presents: The Proving Ground
sources.speaker: Larry Ellison and other race survivors (CNN documentary narration and interviews)
sources.locator: Rush transcript of the documentary. Ellison's passages on reassuring his fiancee, the waves, the finish, and the closing reflection
sources.excerpt: "We had a lead in the race, and no one cared. But everyone cared about the morning, about the sunrise and how incredibly beautiful it was." ... "I guess we didn't listen carefully enough to the warnings that were there. I don't think it was arrogance so much as curiosity." ... "We were at our absolute limits in this storm."
sources.context: Documentary transcript built from interviews with survivors, rescuers and forecasters. Opened; Ellison's passages were read in context. It is a rush transcript and the documentary edits interviews into a narrative, so the order of his remarks is the producers'. Other survivors' accounts in the same film describe the deaths on smaller yachts; Sayonara lost no one.

sources.title: Nervous System: The Strange Case of the Forged Email, the Carphone, and the Woman Who Lost Her Job
sources.speaker: David Kalat, BRG / Legaltech News
sources.locator: Full article: the affair, the April 1993 firing, the disputed email, the $100,000 settlement, the 1996 charges and the January 1997 trial
sources.excerpt: "She sued the company for wrongful termination, alleging she was let go in retaliation for refusing sex to Ellison." ... "Oracle settled the case. Lee got $100,000, a tiny fraction of the billion dollars she had been seeking" ... "Wasserman charged her with multiple felonies, including perjury, preparing false evidence, and altering computer data. Lee pled not guilty. The trial began in January 1997." ... "The jury took less than a day to find Lee guilty on two counts of perjury and two counts of falsifying documents. She was sentenced to a year in jail and ordered to repay the $100,000."
sources.context: Retrospective by a digital-forensics consultant written for a legal-technology column, 25 years after the trial. Opened. It relies partly on Matthew Symonds's Softwar for the email texts and gives Ellison's side more fully than Adelyn Lee's. Contemporaneous court records and 1997 San Francisco Chronicle coverage were not opened. It reports the defence theory that Ellison or someone acting for him planted the email. Ellison's own 2002 account (S03) says she 'later went to jail for a year for perjury and for falsifying evidence'.

sources.title: Ellison to settle insider trading suit
sources.speaker: Computerworld / IDG News Service (quoting plaintiffs' lawyer Joseph Tabacco)
sources.locator: News report, full text
sources.excerpt: "The lawsuit charges that Ellison engaged in insider trading by selling nearly US$900 million in Oracle stock in January 2001, just weeks before the company announced that it would not meet earning expectations for its third fiscal quarter of 2001." ... "Last year a Delaware court found that Oracle's CEO and Jeffrey Henley, formerly Oracle's chief financial officer, were not guilty of insider trading in the matter."
sources.context: Trade-press report of the tentative settlement of the California derivative suit. Opened. The only named source is the plaintiffs' lawyer; Oracle declined to comment. 'Not guilty' is the reporter's loose phrase for a civil ruling in Delaware in Ellison's favour.

sources.title: Court OKs Ellison $22 million shareholder settlement
sources.speaker: InfoWorld / IDG News Service (quoting Joseph Tabacco)
sources.locator: News report, full text
sources.excerpt: "The settlement also requires Ellison to donate $100 million in Oracle's name to charity and to acknowledge that changes were made to Oracle's insider trading policies as a result of the lawsuit" ... "Judge Schwartz rejected the original settlement at a hearing Sept. 26 because he questioned Oracle's role in paying those fees."
sources.context: Follow-up report on court approval. Opened. Same wire service and same plaintiffs' lawyer as S12, so it is not independent corroboration. Oracle spokespeople did not return calls. The article does not report any admission of wrongdoing.

sources.title: Oracle's Ellison blasts HP board for Hurd's exit
sources.speaker: Reuters via NBC News (quoting Larry Ellison's email to the New York Times)
sources.locator: Wire report, first eight paragraphs
sources.excerpt: "The HP board just made the worst personnel decision since the idiots on the Apple board fired Steve Jobs many years ago," Ellison wrote. ... "Publishing known false sexual harassment claims is not good corporate governance; it's cowardly corporate political correctness."
sources.context: Wire report of an email Ellison sent to the New York Times and Oracle then gave to Reuters, days after Hewlett-Packard forced out chief executive Mark Hurd, described as his close friend. Opened. The report says HP's board had determined Hurd did not violate its sexual harassment policy and that the inquiry turned up expense account abuses; it says HP disputed Ellison's account of events and that he did not say how he came by his information. Oracle's later hiring of Hurd is not in this report and is not stated in the article.

sources.title: Larry Ellison: Google is ABSOLUTELY EVIL, but NSA is ESSENTIAL
sources.speaker: Neil McAllister, The Register (quoting Larry Ellison on CBS This Morning with Charlie Rose)
sources.locator: News report of the broadcast interview; NSA and Google passages
sources.excerpt: "It's great, it's essential. President Obama thinks it's essential. It's essential if we want to minimize the kind of strikes that we just had in Boston. It's absolutely essential." ... "We just think they took our stuff and that was wrong. I think what they did was absolutely evil,"
sources.context: Same-day report of a CBS This Morning interview aired August 13, 2013, weeks after the Snowden disclosures. Opened. The Register notes that the NSA is an Oracle customer. The CBS video itself was not viewed, so wording rests on this report.

sources.speaker: Fortune (reporting text messages disclosed in Twitter v. Musk)
sources.locator: Section on funding requests: the April 20, 2022 exchange between Musk and Ellison
sources.excerpt: "Just over an hour later, Ellison responded saying "of course," saying he'd front "whatever you recommend" to Musk." ... "(Ellison eventually settled on $1 billion in funding for the Twitter deal.)"

sources.title: Oracle founder Larry Ellison joined call about contesting Trump's election loss
sources.speaker: Engadget (summarizing Washington Post reporting on court filings in Fair Fight v. True the Vote)
sources.locator: News report, full text
sources.excerpt: "Jim was on a call this evening with Jay Sekulow, Lindsey O. Graham, Sean Hannity, and Larry Ellison," True the Vote's founder, Catherine Engelbrecht, wrote to a donor, according to court filings reviewed by the Post. ... "He has seemingly never expressed doubts about the 2020 election results publicly."
sources.context: Secondary summary of a Washington Post report. Opened. The underlying evidence is a third party's email describing a November 14, 2020 call; it does not record anything Ellison said on the call. The Post article and the court filing were not opened. sources.speaker: Fortune / Bloomberg (citing people familiar with the protest)
sources.locator: News report, first five paragraphs
sources.excerpt: "People left their desks Thursday at Oracle offices around the world to protest Chairman Larry Ellison's fundraiser a day earlier for President Donald Trump, according to people familiar with the matter. The protest, called No Ethics/No Work, involved about 300 employees"
sources.context: Report of the February 20, 2020 employee protest that followed a Trump re-election fundraiser at Ellison's Rancho Mirage estate. Opened. sources.title: Billionaire Larry Ellison says a vast AI-fueled surveillance system can ensure 'citizens will be on their best behavior'
sources.speaker: Kenneth Niemeyer, Business Insider (quoting Larry Ellison at an Oracle financial analyst meeting)
sources.locator: News report, opening paragraphs (text visible before the subscriber wall)

sources.context: Report of remarks Ellison made to investors at Oracle's September 2024 financial analyst meeting, at age 80. The opening paragraphs with the quotation were readable; the rest is behind a subscriber wall. The reporter's framing ('gleefully', 'surveillance dystopia') is editorial. Oracle's own recording of the meeting was not opened, so the fuller context of the remark (police body cameras and school safety) is not verified here.

"Last week, WBD directors dismissed Paramount's funding as "illusory," citing concerns that the capital was tied to a "revocable family trust"

The quoted words are the company's, not Ellison's; he made no public comment in the article. 'Comes to his son's rescue' is the headline writer's framing.

claims.claim: Ellison says he was born in New York City in 1944 to an unmarried 19-year-old mother and at nine months was adopted by her aunt and uncle in Chicago, where he grew up on the South Side.
claims.passage: By his own account, Ellison was born in New York City in 1944 to an unmarried 19-year-old who could not care for him. At nine months he went to her aunt and uncle on Chicago's South Side.
claims.inference: Biographical frame. The birth year is in his own words ('I was born in 1944', 1995); the full date is the Academy's. The adoption story is his own account, repeated consistently in 1997 and 2004.
claims.alternative: No independent record of the adoption was opened. The Academy says the Bronx; he says 'New York City' and 'the lower east side of Manhattan'. Use 'New York City'.

claims.claim: Ellison says his adoptive father, Louis Ellison, routinely told him he would 'never amount to anything', which he described, laughing, as 'an alternative greeting'.
claims.passage: On CBS he recalled being told he would "never amount to anything," and described it, laughing, as "an alternative greeting as opposed to, 'Hi, how are you?'"
claims.inference: Establishes what he says about the relationship, in a joking register, at age 59. He repeats the 'disadvantages' line in 2002, crediting Tim Rice.
claims.alternative: Only Ellison's side exists in opened sources; Louis Ellison died before any of these interviews. Whether the father's dismissal caused his drive is his biographers' theory, which he partly accepts and partly deflects. Do not write it as a proven childhood wound.

claims.claim: In the 1997 Academy of Achievement interview Ellison said the most important aspect of his personality, 'as far as determining my success goes', was questioning conventional wisdom, doubting the experts and questioning authority.
claims.passage: In 1997 he named the trait that had most determined his success: "questioning conventional wisdom, doubting the experts, and questioning authority."
claims.inference: His own account of the root of his character puts resistance to authority first, before ambition or image. This is the earliest and most stable theme in the record.
claims.alternative: He is naming the trait he credits for his success, not describing his whole personality, and the repair words the lead-in that way (verify-05). It is a self-description given to an admiring audience.

claims.claim: Ellison's adoptive mother died during the final exams of his second year at the University of Illinois, and he dropped out, according to the Academy of Achievement's biography.
claims.passage: She died during his second year at the University of Illinois, and he left
claims.inference: A biographical fact stated without a causal claim. It identifies the mother in the six-year-old memory as the adoptive mother who raised him and later died while he was at college.
claims.alternative: A staff-written institutional biography that is not independent of his own account. No independent record was opened.

claims.claim: In 1995 Ellison explained founding his company by saying the leaders he had worked for ran their companies out of business: 'next time, if the company was going to go down, I was going to be out front.'
claims.passage: "I can run a company out of business all by myself. So I thought, next time, if the company was going to go down, I was going to be out front."
claims.inference: The stated motive for the central act of his life is autonomy and control of his environment, said before and after he became one of the richest people alive. He does not say he started the company to be rich, admired or first.
claims.alternative: Founders often retell their motives modestly. In 1995 he also says the goal was a place of 'mutual respect and mutual affection', a warmer motive than control. The two accounts agree on leaving bosses he thought less capable.

claims.claim: Asked about fear of failure in 1997, Ellison said it 'drives me to make sure that my life is orderly, that I'm in control of my company, or in control of the airplane or boat or what-have-you, so that I'm not at risk of failure', and that when he feels close to failure 'I can't stop working'.
claims.passage: "It drives me to make sure that my life is orderly, that I'm in control of my company, or in control of the airplane or boat or what-have-you, so that I'm not at risk of failure."
claims.inference: He names fear of failure as his driver, then describes his answer to it as taking control. The response to the fear is the discriminating detail: control of the thing, not management of how it looks.
claims.alternative: Fear of failure as the stated engine is classic Type 3 language, and overwork under threat fits a 3 as well. This passage supports both readings and is the hinge of the 8-versus-3 question.

claims.claim: The line 'It is not sufficient that I succeed; everyone else must fail' is widely attributed to Ellison. He says a Japanese executive said it to him, citing Genghis Khan, that he retold the story at Oracle, and that the New York Times printed it as his own 'out of context'.
claims.passage: The line most attached to Ellison is that "it is not sufficient that I succeed; everyone else must fail." He says it isn't his.
claims.inference: A fidelity caution for the draft and a small piece of evidence: he took the lesson (pursue market share relentlessly) while disowning the sentence. CBS in 2004 still called it his 'favorite saying'.
claims.alternative: He admired the idea enough to repeat it for years, so the distinction between quoting and endorsing is thin. The original Times article was not opened.

claims.claim: On CBS in 2004 Ellison told a story in which his sister asked whether it was more important 'to be admired or be loved', he chose admired, and she told him he was wrong.
claims.passage: "When I was a kid, my sister walked into my room and said, 'Larry, which is more important to you – to be admired or be loved?' And I said, 'Well, for me personally? To be admired.' She looks at me, smiles, 'Wrong,' and walks out."
claims.inference: Strong evidence for the Type 3 alternative in the 'admired' telling, and for an 8-style guard over tenderness in the 'respected' telling. The two wordings matter and must not be merged.
claims.alternative: The story is from his mid-teens, retold 40 years later with two different key words. It shows how he narrates himself, not what he felt at 15.
claims.review_trigger: Confirm the original 60 Minutes II air date; the text now cites only the CBS web publication in February 2004 and gives no age.

claims.claim: In 2002 Ellison said that without unconditional love from parents 'you have a great void in your life', that 'you can get very good at trying to earn the love of others', and 'Bill Clinton is like me in that regard.'
claims.passage: "If you don't get unconditional love early on, you have a great void in your life." He went on, "Depending on how you adapt, you can get very good at trying to earn the love of others. Bill Clinton is like me in that regard."
claims.inference: He applies the earned-love description to himself in the first person. The article now counts this for Type 3 at face value.
claims.alternative: The question was leading (whether he was out to prove his father wrong), but he accepted the premise, and the next exchange (C99) shows him answering as if the void were his own.

claims.claim: Asked in 2004 who he is winning for, Ellison said: 'I admit to it, mea culpa. An awful lot of it is personal vanity.'
claims.passage: "I admit to it, mea culpa. An awful lot of it is personal vanity."
claims.inference: He concedes vanity plainly, which supports the Type 3 alternative, and fuses his own limits with the company's.
claims.alternative: A disarming admission on television can itself be a way of controlling the interview.

claims.claim: In 2002 Ellison said: 'Not conforming caused terrible problems for me at school, but it was magic in business.'
claims.passage: "Not conforming caused terrible problems for me at school, but it was magic in business,"
claims.inference: By his own account nonconformity is a method that pays. The article says so and no longer presents his defiance as a price he pays in approval.
claims.alternative: The answer continues: 'The only way you can succeed in business big-time is to find places where conventional wisdom is wrong.' A Type 3 whose brand is the contrarian winner could say the same. The 1997 'fashion and the pursuit of love' line was cut in the edit.

claims.claim: In the 1997 interview, while listing notable people that fame had let him meet, Ellison defended Michael Milken, who had served prison time: 'It's not terribly fashionable to be a supporter of Michael Milken, but I'm honored to have him as my friend.'
claims.passage: "It's not terribly fashionable to be a supporter of Michael Milken, but I'm honored to have him as my friend," he said.
claims.inference: Shows him restating loyalty to a disgraced friend in public. It is no longer counted as approval given up for nothing, because the two were business partners at the time (C98).
claims.alternative: The interview is edited, so what prompted the remark cannot be known. He also said Milken was jailed 'because of someone's political advantage'. Defending a current business partner is self-interested as well as loyal.

claims.claim: At a press conference on June 28, 2000 about Oracle's hired detectives, Ellison called the investigation 'a public service' and said: 'We will ship our garbage to Redmond, and they can go through it. We believe in full disclosure.'
claims.passage: he offered to ship Oracle's garbage to Microsoft: "We believe in full disclosure."
claims.inference: Faced with an embarrassing disclosure, he neither denied nor distanced himself. He claimed it, went on offence and repeated the defence for two years. This is the clearest observed case of choosing the fight over reputation.
claims.alternative: Owning a scandal loudly can be shrewd reputation management for a self-styled outlaw, and the story hurt Microsoft too. Oracle also funded advocacy groups of its own, which he did not mention.

claims.claim: Oracle posted its first losses in 1990 and came close to failing. Asked in 2002 about the crash, Ellison said: 'I wasn't a very good CEO.'
claims.passage: "I wasn't a very good CEO," he said of Oracle's near-collapse in the early 1990s.
claims.inference: When the company was failing he took direct charge and removed people he felt loyal to. He also admits fault in plain words, which complicates the picture of a man who cannot concede error.
claims.alternative: Both statements were made years later from a position of recovery. The Academy says Oracle's sales staff had 'habitually overstated revenues'; Ellison's own role in that culture is not examined in opened sources.

claims.claim: Andy Grove, described by Fortune in 2000 as Ellison's pal, said: 'He works very hard at his bad-boy image.'
claims.passage: "He works very hard at his bad-boy image."
claims.inference: Third-party testimony from a friend that the persona is managed. It is the best outside evidence for the Type 3 alternative.
claims.alternative: A one-line remark in a single profile. Grove was teasing a friend.

claims.claim: Ray Lane, Oracle's second-in-command until Ellison pushed him out, described the culture on CBS in 2004: 'Culture is win at any cost.'
claims.passage: Lane told CBS, "Culture is win at any cost,"
claims.inference: Named testimony about how his drive lands on others: the cost of the pattern is paid by subordinates.
claims.alternative: Lane had been forced out and is not a neutral witness. The 2000 date of his departure comes from the Fortune profile and the research record.

claims.claim: In August 2010, after Hewlett-Packard forced out chief executive Mark Hurd, a close friend, Ellison emailed the New York Times: 'The HP board just made the worst personnel decision since the idiots on the Apple board fired Steve Jobs many years ago.' The report says HP's board had determined Hurd did not violate its sexual harassment policy and that the inquiry turned up expense account abuses.
claims.passage: that its board had made the worst personnel decision since "the idiots on the Apple board" fired Steve Jobs
claims.inference: He publicly attacked a major business partner's board to defend a friend in disgrace, then put him on the payroll. It is a second instance of loud loyalty that carries reputational and commercial risk.
claims.alternative: Attacking a competitor's board also served Oracle. HP disputed his account of events, and he called the harassment claim 'known false' without saying how he knew.

claims.claim: When Elon Musk texted on April 20, 2022 asking whether he would join the Twitter purchase, Ellison replied 'of course' and offered 'whatever you recommend', as Fortune reported from court-disclosed texts. Musk proposed $2 billion 'or more'; Ellison settled on $1 billion.
claims.passage: He replied "of course" and offered "whatever you recommend,"
claims.inference: A private message with no audience expected. It shows quick backing for someone in his circle and nothing more: he committed half the suggested sum to a deal other investors wanted into.
claims.alternative: No cost or risk to him is shown, so it is weak type evidence. Exact wording varies between outlets.
claims.review_trigger: Take the exact Musk-Ellison messages from the Twitter v. Musk court exhibit and correct the quotation if it differs from Fortune's summary.

claims.claim: On December 22, 2025 Paramount Skydance announced that Larry Ellison had provided an 'irrevocable personal guarantee' of $40.4 billion for its bid for Warner Bros. Discovery and had agreed not to revoke the family trust. He was 81.

claims.claim: The profile's type thesis: Ellison is best read as an Enneagram Type 8 at medium confidence, because control of his surroundings is the motive he names and under criticism he does not retreat; Type 3 is the strongest alternative.

The record supports that he names control as his motive in three interviews (a fourth, on marriage, is weaker), that he restates his purpose and attacks when criticized, and that a former deputy and a biographer describe conduct that secures control without adding admirers (C132 to C135). It also supports, through three reviews of Wilson's biography, that he improved his own story (C129 to C131), which the article counts for Type 3 and uses to discount every self-report.
claims.alternative: A Type 3 whose brand is the unapologetic winner would behave the same way in public (C21). Reviewers report that Wilson's biography documents invented self-flattering details, which is image evidence in its own right. Lane was ousted and Wilson is read only through reviews. Both biographies are unread.

claims.claim: The discriminator between Type 8 and Type 3: public conduct cannot separate the two readings and the reported inventions discount his self-reports on both sides, so the case for Type 8 rests on conduct other people describe (pushing out his second-in-command of eight years, a culture that treated the rest as 'weak soldiers', a biographer's 'he had to humiliate them'), which secures control and adds no admiration; that evidence is thin.
claims.passage: What keeps Type 8 ahead is what other people describe him doing, and there is less of it than a confident typing would want.
claims.inference: The repair replaces 'evidence that does not depend on an audience' (four self-reports and one text) with third-party conduct, because the embellishment record weakens self-report. Winning earns admiration; driving out a deputy and humiliating the beaten do not, and a reading built on admiration does not predict them. The control self-reports and the private text remain as secondary support with their limits stated.
claims.alternative: Lane was forced out and is not neutral. The 'humiliate' sentence is Wilson's, read through a review whose archived copy has lost its quotation marks. An unhealthy Three can also be ruthless with subordinates and rivals, and Lane's ouster may have been about credit as much as control. The article says Type 3 stays live and keeps confidence at medium.

type_hypothesis.against: The strongest evidence against Type 8 is in Ellison's own words. He says people deprived of unconditional love learn to earn it and adds 'Bill Clinton is like me in that regard' (C14); asked whether achievements fill the void he says 'Yes and no' and tells the sister story as his answer (C99). In one telling he chose being 'admired' over being loved (C13). He admits 'An awful lot of it is personal vanity' (C15). He names fear of failure, not anger, as what drives him (C53), and his first and last answer to that fear is overwork (C94, C95). Fortune reported that passing Gates as the richest man might matter to him more than Oracle's dominance (C102), and he says what means a lot to him is Oracle passing Microsoft (C103). Andy Grove, a friend, said he 'works very hard at his bad-boy image' (C21). The injury he names from the Lee accusation is how a stranger looked at him (C70), and his signature story changes its key word between tellings (C13, C46). The friend he defended as unfashionable was his business partner (C98). By his own account nonconformity is 'magic in business' (C16), a winning method and not a price. He concedes fault readily (C19). His support for state surveillance and his trust in government protection (C30, C74, C75) are not the anti-authority stance usually expected of an Eight and lean toward Type 6. Weighed in the repair: three opened reviews of Mike Wilson's 1997 biography report that he improved his own story. Kirkus says he grew up on middle-class South Shore Drive but 'has told reporters that he lived in the South Side ghetto' and would 'imply he had an advanced degree in physics' (C129); Publishers Weekly says he has no college degree, 'let alone the graduate degrees attributed to him' (C130); Computergram relays a friend from his early Chicago years saying he 'made up delightful and often plausible details' in stories that 'glorified Larry Ellison' (C132) and an ex-employee's 'Larry always had a problem with tenses'. The 1997 interview the profile relies on carries a version of the origin claim (C131). Self-flattering invention is image evidence in its own right, and it lowers the weight of every self-report, including the four control statements the edit leaned on. The same review quotes Wilson's theme that Ellison, like Citizen Kane, 'wants desperately to be loved, even idolized', which also points to Type 3. His marriage remark, read in full, describes holding a partner to his own standard, which fits a One or a Three as well as an Eight (C37).
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 3, the achiever: a boy told he would 'never amount to anything' (C02) who says love had to be earned and applies that to himself (C14, C99), who wanted to be admired (C13), admits vanity (C15), answers fear of failure with overwork (C94, C95), wants to be number one (C102, C103) and works at a bad-boy image (C21). Reviewers of Wilson's biography add outside evidence: invented or inflated details about his origins and schooling, in stories a friend said 'glorified Larry Ellison' (C129, C130, C132). The decisive point for this reading is that a Three courts the audience whose admiration he wants, and Ellison's audience admires a fighter who never apologizes, so every public episode of defiance is consistent with Type 3. Type 6 is the third reading and is tested in the article: fear named as the engine, order and control as the remedy, a lifelong habit of doubting experts, and trust in government protection over 'blind luck' (C30). What leans away from Six is that his remedy for risk is his own control and that when a rule bound him personally he ignored it and beat it in court (C104). Type 7 was also considered for his appetite for adventure and novelty and his reframing of pain. It ranks fourth: he describes risk as a test of his limits, went back to a race that had already battered him, and says the 1998 storm made him more cautious (C107). The article's Type 7 paragraph was cut in the edit because its only test was his tenure at Oracle, which does not separate the types.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: Public conduct does not separate Type 8 from Type 3, and the article says so: criticized, he restates his purpose and attacks (C18, C97, C24), and a Three whose audience admires a fighter would do the same. The repair also weighs the reported record that he improved his own story (C129 to C132); it counts for Type 3 and discounts his self-reports on both sides, the confessions of vanity and earned love as much as the statements about control. What keeps Type 8 ahead is conduct other people describe that secures control and adds no admiration: he pushed out his second-in-command of eight years in a clash over direction (C133), that deputy described a culture in which everyone outside the top tier was a 'weak soldier' (C134), and Wilson, as a review quotes him, wrote that it was not enough for his opponents to lose, 'he had to humiliate them' (C135). Winning earns admiration; driving out a deputy and humiliating the beaten do not (C136). Secondary support: control is the motive he gives for founding the company in 1995 (C07) and 2016 (C50) and as his remedy for fear in 1997 (C08), with a weaker fourth instance on marriage (C37); Fortune cites Wilson's book for a boy who 'bridled under authority' (C137); when a rule bound him personally he ignored it and beat it in court (C104); and one private text shows quick backing for a member of his circle at no cost (C25, C140). Limits: Lane was ousted and is not neutral; Wilson is read only through reviews; an unhealthy Three can be ruthless too; both biographies and the testimony of intimates remain unread. The margin is narrow. Confidence stays medium, and C47, C58, C136 and C138 are marked unresolved until the books are read.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: Several things do not sit neatly in a Type 8 reading. The one deep fear he admits is a six-year-old's dread that his adoptive mother would not come home (C40), and he says outright that he conceals how much being loved matters (C46). He gives fear of failure, not anger or strength, as his engine (C53), and the article concedes that the core-emotion evidence for Type 8 is thin (C91). An interviewer who expected a bully found him 'warm and self-effacing' (C66). He champions surveillance by the state and says he would rather trust the government than luck while describing himself as a lifelong questioner of authority, and the father he says he defined himself against held much the same trust (C30, C115). By his own 2016 account he deferred to Steve Jobs over Apple in 1995, a story left out of the article as single-source. His telling of his sister's question changes between 'admired' and 'respected' (C13, C46), and the article says the record does not settle which he wanted more. Whether the swagger is the man or a role he plays well is not settled by the opened record.
